glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Proverbs 14 sets the wise woman who builds her house against the foolish one who tears hers down, warns that a way can seem right and still end in death, and finds in the fear of the LORD both strong confidence and a fountain of life.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Solomon’s short contrasting sayings continue (10:1–22:16). The words chapter 13 used for the teaching of the wise, “a fountain of life” (13:14), return here for the fear of the LORD (14:27).

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “There is a way that seems right to a man, But its end is the way of death.” (Proverbs 14:12)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Proverbs 14 begins with a woman and a house: “The wise woman builds her house, But the foolish pulls it down with her hands” (14:1). Her house recalls the one Wisdom built (9:1) and looks ahead to the woman of valor (31:10–31). Whatever a life builds, a home, a marriage, or a livelihood, carries the signature of the wisdom or folly behind it, and the foolish woman’s ruin is her own work.

The middle of the chapter questions what feels certain. “There is a way that seems right to a man, But its end is the way of death” (14:12), repeated word for word at 16:25. Fools laugh off their guilt (14:9), the simple believe every word (14:15), and a laughing face can hide a sorrowing heart (14:13). Because feelings and appearances mislead, the prudent man “considers well his steps.”

Against that uncertainty the chapter sets something firm: “In the fear of the LORD there is strong confidence” (14:26). The right view of God that turns the wise from evil (14:16) also gives His children refuge, and it is “a fountain of life” (14:27). The same God stands behind the poor: “He who oppresses the poor reproaches his Maker” (14:31). Seeing Him rightly changes how a person treats the neighbor others avoid (14:20–21), and such righteousness “exalts a nation” (14:34).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Proverbs 14:1–7 — The Wise Woman Builds Her House

The chapter’s first picture is a house built up or pulled down by the woman who lives in it, and the sayings that follow show wisdom at work in an upright walk that reveals what a person thinks of God, in lips that protect the wise, and in the untidy stable where an ox’s strength brings a larger harvest. The section closes with a scoffer who seeks wisdom without finding it and with the counsel to walk away from a man whose lips carry no knowledge.

Proverbs 14:8–15 — The Way That Seems Right

The prudent man studies his own road, while fools deceive themselves and laugh off their guilt, and at the center stands the warning that a road can feel right and still lead to death. Around it the sayings look inward, to a heart whose bitterness and joy no stranger fully shares, to laughter that can cover sorrow, and to the simple who believe every word while the prudent weigh each step.

Proverbs 14:16–25 — Prudence, Mercy to the Poor, and a True Witness

The wise man fears evil enough to turn from it, while the fool rages ahead in self-confidence, the quick-tempered act rashly, and the simple inherit folly by drifting. The section then speaks honestly about how the poor are shunned, calls despising a neighbor sin, blesses the one who shows mercy, and prizes labor over idle chatter and the true witness whose testimony saves lives.

Proverbs 14:26–27 — The Fear of the LORD Is a Fountain of Life

Two sayings name the fear of the LORD as strong confidence and a refuge for His children, and as a spring that keeps turning a person away from the snares of death. The right view of God that makes the defiant tremble is the same view that gives those who fear Him a safe place to stand.

Proverbs 14:28–35 — Righteousness Exalts a Nation

Sayings about the king frame the last section, measuring a ruler’s honor by the people he governs and his favor by the wisdom of his servants. Between them stand the patient man and the sound heart, the poor whose treatment honors or insults their Maker, the righteous who have refuge even in death, and the righteousness that lifts up a whole nation.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Proverbs 14 warns that sincerity cannot certify a road. A person can feel sure, follow what seems right, and still arrive at death (14:12), which is why the chapter keeps calling for a prudence that tests words and watches steps (14:8, 15). Jesus describes the same danger: “broad is the way that leads to destruction” (Matthew 7:13).

The chapter also ties honor toward God to the treatment of the poor. The rich gather friends while the poor man is avoided even by his neighbor (14:20), yet mercy to the needy honors their Maker and oppression insults Him (14:31). Alongside this, the sayings on hidden bitterness and sorrow (14:10, 13) teach a compassion that does not judge a person by the surface.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Building and tearing down. The wise build a house that lasts, folly pulls down its own, and the house of the wicked is overthrown while the tent of the upright flourishes (14:1, 11).

The way that seems right. The prudent understand their way and consider their steps, while the simple believe every word and a confident path can still end in death (14:8, 12, 15).

The hidden heart. Bitterness, joy, envy, and sorrow lie deeper than others can see, while wisdom rests quietly in the heart of the one who understands (14:10, 13, 30, 33).

Mercy to the poor. Despising a neighbor is sin, and how a person treats the poor is how he treats their Maker (14:20–21, 31).

Truthful testimony. A faithful witness does not lie, and a true witness delivers souls, while a false one pours out lies (14:5, 25).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
The wise woman (14:1). A woman whose wisdom builds up her household. She echoes Wisdom, who “has built her house” (9:1), and anticipates the woman of valor (31:10–31). The saying calls every reader to examine what he or she is building; it does not blame women for every troubled home.

The scoffer (14:6). The one who will not be taught (9:7–8; 13:1). Here he even goes looking for wisdom, but his contempt for correction keeps him from finding it, while knowledge comes easily to a teachable heart.

The backslider in heart (14:14). A person who has turned away inwardly, whatever his outward life may still look like. He is filled with the fruit of his own ways, while a good man is satisfied from above.

The simple and the prudent (14:15, 18). The simple are uncommitted and easily led, so they believe whatever they hear and inherit folly by drifting. The prudent have practical good sense and are “crowned with knowledge” (14:18), the prudence Proverbs was written to give the simple (1:4).

The fear of the LORD (14:26–27). A right view of God. For those who defy Him it means terror, and for all it means awe at His holiness, His being unlike any other. That same awe makes His children secure, because the God they revere is their refuge.

A refuge in his death (14:32). The righteous have a place of safety in God that death cannot take away. The ancient Greek translation reads the line differently, but the NKJV wording most likely expresses hope that reaches beyond the grave.

sections.title: The Wise Woman Builds Her House
Prudence, Mercy to the Poor, and a True Witness
The Fear of the LORD Is a Fountain of Life

1.brief: Wisdom builds and folly tears down, pictured here in two women and their homes: the wise woman builds her house, while the foolish one pulls hers down with her own hands. The saying recalls Wisdom building her house in 9:1 and looks ahead to the woman of valor in 31:10–31, and whatever is built in a life bears the signature of the wisdom or folly behind it.
1.explain:
“The wise woman builds her house,”

The chapter opens with a woman at work on her household. Her “house” is more than a building; it is the home and family she tends, its peace, its provision, and its future. Her wisdom shows in what she builds. Readers of Proverbs have heard this language before: “Wisdom has built her house” (9:1). The wise woman does in a single home what Wisdom does on a grand scale, and the book will close with a portrait of such a woman, who “watches over the ways of her household” (31:27). Whatever is built in a life, a marriage, a family, finances, a ministry, bears the signature of the wisdom behind it.

“But the foolish pulls it down with her hands.”

The foolish woman also has a house, and she tears it down. No enemy has to break in; she does the damage “with her hands,” through her own words, habits, and choices. The contrast stands within the book’s larger picture of two women and two houses, Wisdom and Folly, each calling to the simple. The saying is not a judgment on women in general, nor does it blame every wife or mother for every troubled home. It holds up a mirror to every reader, man or woman, and asks what his or her own hands are doing to the house God has given.
1.notes:
The Hebrew opens with a plural, literally the wise ones of women, which is why ESV has “wisest” and KJV and YLT add “Every.” The NKJV’s singular gives the same sense: the line describes the kind of woman who builds her house.

The second line in Hebrew begins with the ordinary noun for folly rather than a word for a foolish woman. That is why ESV reads the line as folly itself tearing the house down, a reading that strengthens the echo of Wisdom and Folly in chapter 9.

2.brief: A person’s daily walk shows what he thinks of God. The one who lives uprightly fears the LORD, while the one whose ways are crooked despises Him, whatever he may claim with his lips.
2.explain:
“He who walks in his uprightness fears the LORD,”

A person’s walk is his daily conduct, the way he lives when no one is checking. The one who walks in uprightness, straight and honest in his dealings, fears the LORD. The saying works in both directions. The fear of the LORD, a right view of God, produces upright living, and upright living shows that the fear of the LORD is really there. Reverence for God is not hidden in the heart only; it comes out in the feet.

“But he who is perverse in his ways despises Him.”

The perverse person is crooked and devious in his ways. Whatever he may say about God, his life despises Him. He treats God’s commands and God Himself as if they did not matter. The two lines make a person’s conduct the clearest testimony to what he truly thinks of God. A crooked way of life is not merely a moral failing; at its root it is contempt for the LORD.
2.notes: ESV and NASB render “perverse” as “devious,” describing a person whose ways turn aside from what is straight.

3.brief: In a fool’s mouth pride becomes a rod, and his arrogant words end up bringing punishment on himself. The lips of the wise protect them, because careful speech keeps them out of harm.
3.explain:
“In the mouth of a fool is a rod of pride,”

The fool’s mouth holds a rod, and the rod is made of pride. His arrogant, boastful words become a stick that strikes others and eventually brings punishment back on him. Proverbs speaks elsewhere of the rod that falls on the fool: “a rod is for the back of him who is devoid of understanding” (10:13). Here the fool supplies that rod himself. His proud talk is the very thing that will bring correction down on his own back.

“But the lips of the wise will preserve them.”

The wise also have mouths, but their lips protect them. Careful, humble speech keeps them out of the trouble that the fool’s pride invites. The contrast continues the theme of guarded speech from 13:3. The fool is undone by what he says; the wise are kept safe by what they say and by what they refrain from saying.
3.notes:
The Hebrew word for “rod” here is not the word for rod used in 13:24. It is a different word that refers to a shoot or branch rather than a staff, so the fool’s proud words are pictured as a stick that grows out of his own mouth.

Several modern translations read the first line as a rod for the fool’s “back” (ESV, NASB), following a slightly different understanding of the Hebrew. The NKJV, with KJV and YLT, reads “a rod of pride.”

4.brief: Where there are no oxen, the feeding trough stays clean, but much increase comes by the strength of an ox. Oxen must be fed and cleaned up after, yet their strength makes a far larger harvest possible, and wisdom accepts the costs that come with productive work.
4.explain:
“Where no oxen are, the trough is clean;”

A farmer without oxen has a clean feeding trough. There is no feed to buy, no stall to muck out, no animal to tend. The line is a plain observation from farm life, and it is meant to be smiled at: the cleanest barn belongs to the farmer who is not producing much.

“But much increase comes by the strength of an ox.”

The second line gives the other side. Oxen are messy and expensive, but their strength pulls the plow and brings in a much larger harvest. The saying teaches that productive work carries costs, and wisdom accepts them. A person who avoids every mess and every expense may keep things tidy, but he will also have little to show. The proverb fits far beyond farming: any household, business, or ministry that grows will have its untidy and costly side, and the wise do not mistake a clean trough for success.
4.notes: The Hebrew word behind “clean” can also mean empty, and the 1984 NIV renders it “empty”: without oxen the manger has no grain in it. Either way the picture is of a farm that produces little. ESV, NASB, and KJV read “manger” or “crib” for “trough.”

5.brief: Truth can be expected from a faithful witness. A false witness pours out lies, so the character of each shows itself in what he says when the truth matters most.
5.explain:
“A faithful witness does not lie,”

The setting is the court, where justice depended on the testimony of witnesses. A faithful witness is a reliable one, and his reliability shows itself in the simplest way: he does not lie. When the truth matters most and lying might help a friend or harm an enemy, he tells what he knows. The Law forbade false witness (Exodus 20:16), and Proverbs treats honest testimony as a mark of character.

“But a false witness will utter lies.”

The false witness pours out lies as naturally as breathing. Among the things the LORD hates is “A false witness who speaks lies” (6:19). The two lines are close to saying the same thing twice, and that is the point: what a person is shows in what he says. A faithful man produces true testimony and a false man produces lies, and the court, and everyone else, can know the tree by its fruit. The theme returns at 14:25, where true testimony is shown to save lives.
5.notes: The Hebrew behind “will utter lies” is literally breathes out lies, as ESV and YLT render it, picturing lies that come as easily as breath. Proverbs uses the same Hebrew expression in 6:19, 14:25, 19:5, and 19:9, where the NKJV has “speaks lies.”

6.brief: The scoffer may go looking for wisdom, but his contempt for correction keeps him from ever finding it. To the person who understands, knowledge comes easily, because a teachable heart opens the door that scorn keeps shut.
6.explain:
“A scoffer seeks wisdom and does not find it,”

The scoffer may actually go looking for wisdom. He may want the advantages it brings or the reputation of being wise. Yet he does not find it. The reason lies in what he is. Wisdom begins with the fear of the LORD and grows through correction, and the scoffer has contempt for both (13:1). He wants wisdom on his own terms, without humility, and on those terms it cannot be had.

“But knowledge is easy to him who understands.”

To the person with understanding, knowledge comes easily. He is teachable, so each lesson builds on the last. The contrast is not between a clever person and a dull one. It is between a heart that is open and a heart that is closed. The scoffer’s search is endless and empty because his scorn shuts the door; the understanding person finds the door already open.
6.notes: The NKJV supplies “find it” in the first line; the Hebrew says simply that the scoffer seeks wisdom and there is none, as YLT shows. ESV reads “in vain.”

7.brief: When a man’s lips show no knowledge, the son is told to leave his presence. Staying near such a fool brings nothing good, so wisdom knows when to walk away.
7.explain:
“Go from the presence of a foolish man,”

The saying is a command, the father’s voice speaking directly to his son. Leave the fool’s company. The fool here is the one whose life and talk are set against wisdom. Staying near him will teach nothing good and may draw the son into his ways, as 13:20 warned: “the companion of fools will be destroyed.”

“When you do not perceive in him the lips of knowledge.”

The second line gives the reason and the test. When a man’s words show no knowledge, when a son has listened long enough to see that nothing true or wise is coming, it is time to go. Wisdom does not require endless argument with someone who will not learn. It knows when to walk away. The verse closes the first section with practical counsel about the company a person keeps.
7.notes: The Hebrew of the second line is compressed, and translations handle it differently. NASB reads it as a consequence of staying, warning that the son will not discern words of knowledge, and ESV as a reason for leaving. The NKJV, with KJV, makes it a condition: leave when you see no knowledge in him.

8.brief: The prudent man’s wisdom lies in understanding his own way, thinking about where his steps are taking him. Fools are marked by deceit, misleading others and themselves about the road they are on.
8.explain:
“The wisdom of the prudent is to understand his way,”

The prudent person’s wisdom is pointed at his own path. He thinks about where his steps are taking him, why he is going that way, and where the road ends. This is wisdom turned inward, the honest self-examination that keeps a person from drifting. It opens a section of the chapter that keeps returning to the idea of a way and its end (14:12, 14, 15).

“But the folly of fools is deceit.”

Fools are marked by deceit. They mislead others, and, more dangerously, they mislead themselves about the road they are on. The contrast with the first line suggests that self-deception is especially in view: where the prudent man looks honestly at his way, the fool tells himself a comfortable story. That is how a person can walk confidently down a path that ends in death, the warning that comes four verses later (14:12).
8.notes: The NLT draws out the self-deception the contrast implies: “fools deceive themselves.” ESV renders the last word “deceiving.”

9.brief: Fools treat sin as a joke and mock at the guilt it brings. Among the upright there is favor, the goodwill that grows where people deal honestly and make things right.
9.explain:
“Fools mock at sin,”

Fools treat sin as a joke. They laugh off wrongdoing and the guilt it brings, and they make light of any effort to make things right. Mockery of this kind stands in the way of the very things that would help: honestly admitting the wrong and making amends for it. The fool’s laughter keeps him exactly where he is.

“But among the upright there is favor.”

Among the upright there is favor, goodwill and acceptance. Upright people take wrongdoing seriously, admit their faults, and make amends, and so relationships among them can be restored. The contrast is between a company where guilt is laughed off and trust erodes and a company where guilt is faced and goodwill grows. Favor here may include God’s favor as well as human goodwill, for the upright are “His delight” (12:22).
9.notes:
The Hebrew word translated “sin” here is the word used for the guilt offering, the sacrifice brought to make amends for wrongdoing. ESV and YLT render it as the guilt offering, and the 1984 NIV speaks of making amends for sin. Read that way, the fool mocks the very means of setting things right.

The Hebrew of the first line is grammatically unusual: the subject, “fools,” is plural, but the verb “mock” is singular. Because of this, the translators’ notes in the NET Bible discuss a proposal to reverse the line so that the guilt offering is the subject and it mocks fools. The NKJV, like the other translations compared here, keeps fools as the ones who mock.

10.brief: Every heart knows its own bitterness in a way no one else can fully share, and its deepest joys are just as private. The saying recognizes an inner life that others cannot see, which calls for compassion and humility in judging another person.
10.explain:
“The heart knows its own bitterness,”

Every heart carries griefs that only it fully knows. Others may see the outward circumstances, but the bitterness itself, the particular weight of a loss or a wound, is known from the inside. The saying does not tell a person to keep his sorrows to himself; it simply recognizes that there is an inner life no one else can completely enter.

“And a stranger does not share its joy.”

The same is true of joy. The deepest gladness of a heart cannot be fully handed to someone else. A stranger, someone outside, can rejoice with a person but cannot feel exactly what he feels. The verse calls for humility in judging others, since we never see the whole of another person’s heart, and for compassion, since everyone carries more than is visible. Only the One who searches hearts knows them completely (1 Samuel 16:7).
10.notes: Behind “its own bitterness” the Hebrew reads literally the bitterness of its soul, describing grief felt at the deepest level of a person. In the second line KJV and YLT say a stranger does not “intermeddle” with the heart’s joy.

11.brief: The wicked may live in a house that looks solid, but it will be overthrown. The upright may live in a mere tent, yet it will flourish, so outward strength is no measure of what will last.
11.explain:
“The house of the wicked will be overthrown,”

The wicked man lives in a house, a solid, permanent dwelling that seems built to last. Yet it will be overthrown. The saying looks past the present appearance to the end. Wickedness undermines what it builds, and a house founded on it cannot stand. An earlier saying put it the same way: “The wicked are overthrown and are no more, But the house of the righteous will stand” (12:7).

“But the tent of the upright will flourish.”

The upright may live in a mere tent, a modest and temporary dwelling, and yet it will flourish. The word “flourish” pictures something growing and blossoming. The irony is deliberate: the stronger-looking dwelling falls and the weaker-looking one thrives. Outward strength is no measure of what will last. The saying continues the chapter’s interest in houses that began in 14:1.
11.notes: KJV renders “tent” as “tabernacle,” the older English word for a tent.

12.brief: A path can seem right to a man and still end in death. Sincerity is no guarantee of safety, and the same saying returns word for word at 16:25, a warning Jesus echoes when He speaks of the broad way that leads to destruction (Matthew 7:13).
12.explain:
“There is a way that seems right to a man,”

The saying begins with a road that looks good. It seems right, straight and sensible from where a man is standing. He is not consciously choosing evil; he is following what feels right to him. That is what makes the way so dangerous. A path chosen by human judgment alone, apart from God’s word, can look entirely reasonable and still be wrong.

“But its end is the way of death.”

The end of that road is death. Sincerity is no guarantee of safety, and a person can be sincerely mistaken all the way to destruction. The saying sits at the center of a section about ways and steps (14:8–15), and its warning explains why the prudent must understand their way (14:8) and consider their steps (14:15). The same saying returns word for word in 16:25, so Proverbs states this warning twice. The verse does not dismiss conscience; it warns against trusting one’s own sense of what is right apart from God. Jesus spoke of the same danger in His picture of the broad way, “wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction” (Matthew 7:13).
12.notes:
Proverbs 16:25 repeats this verse word for word in the NKJV.

The Hebrew behind “seems right” is literally straight before a man, that is, straight in his own eyes. “Its end” translates a Hebrew word for the latter end or outcome, the same word used in 14:13. The Hebrew also has a plural, ways of death, which KJV and YLT preserve.

13.brief: Laughter can cover a sorrowing heart, and mirth can end in grief. Outward cheer is no proof that all is well inside, which is another reason to treat others with care.
13.explain:
“Even in laughter the heart may sorrow,”

Laughter is not always what it seems. A person can laugh with friends while his heart aches. Outward cheer may cover private grief, and those around him may never know. The saying, like 14:10, recognizes the hidden inner life and warns against assuming that a smiling face means all is well.

“And the end of mirth may be grief.”

Mirth itself can end in grief. Joy in this life is mixed and temporary; the party ends and the sorrow that waited outside comes back in. The verse is not cynical about joy, and Proverbs elsewhere praises “A merry heart” (15:13). It is honest about the limits of earthly happiness. Read with 14:10, it calls for compassion toward others, whose laughter may be covering more than we know, and for realism about one’s own heart.
13.notes: “End” here translates the same Hebrew word for the latter end or outcome used in 14:12, a verbal link between the way that ends in death and the mirth that ends in grief.

14.brief: The backslider in heart, the one who has turned away inwardly, will be filled with the fruit of his own ways and get exactly what he chose. A good man is satisfied too, but with what comes from above.
14.explain:
“The backslider in heart will be filled with his own ways,”

The backslider in heart is a person who has turned away inwardly from God and from what is right. His outward life may not yet show it, but his heart has already gone back. The judgment on him is fitting: he “will be filled with his own ways.” He gets exactly what he chose. The ways he preferred to God’s become his whole diet, and he will have his fill of them, along with their consequences.

“But a good man will be satisfied from above.”

A good man is satisfied too, but the source of his satisfaction is different. The NKJV’s “from above” points beyond the man himself to the good that comes to him from God. The two lines set two kinds of fullness side by side. One person is stuffed with the fruit of his own turning away; the other is filled with good that he did not have to produce for himself. Both reap what their lives have sown, and the contrast lies in what each has chosen to live on.
14.notes:
The final phrase in Hebrew is brief, literally from upon him. KJV renders it “from himself,” and NASB and ESV take it to mean that the good man is filled with the fruit of his own good ways, matching the first line. The NKJV’s “from above” is an interpretive rendering that names God as the source.

“Backslider” translates a Hebrew word for one who turns back or turns away; “in heart” shows that the turning has happened inwardly.

15.brief: The simple, uncommitted and easily led, believe every word they hear. The prudent consider their steps with care and test what they hear before acting on it, which is the very prudence Proverbs was written to give the simple (1:4).
15.explain:
“The simple believes every word,”

The simple person in Proverbs is uncommitted and easily led. He has not set himself against wisdom, but he has not committed himself to it either, and so he believes whatever he hears. Every word sounds convincing to him, the salesman’s pitch, the gossip’s story, the tempter’s promise. His credulity is not innocence; it leaves him exposed to every voice that wants to lead him somewhere.

“But the prudent considers well his steps.”

The prudent person tests what he hears before acting on it. He considers where each step will lead, much like the prudent man of 14:8 who understands his way. The contrast is between drifting and walking with care. Proverbs holds out real hope for the simple, for the book was written “To give prudence to the simple” (1:4). The section ends where it began, with the need to look carefully at one’s path, which is how a person avoids the way that only seems right (14:12).
15.notes: ESV and NASB render “every word” as “everything.” KJV says the prudent man “looketh well” to his going.

16.brief: A wise man fears evil and turns away from it. The fool charges ahead, raging and sure of himself, blind to the danger he refuses to fear.
16.explain:
“A wise man fears and departs from evil,”

The wise man is cautious about evil. He takes its danger seriously, and that healthy fear leads him to turn away from it. Proverbs joins the two elsewhere: “Fear the LORD and depart from evil” (3:7). The wise do not test how close they can come to sin without being harmed; they see where it leads and keep their distance.

“But a fool rages and is self-confident.”

The fool does the opposite. He “rages,” charging ahead with angry, careless energy, and he is self-confident, sure that nothing bad will happen to him. His confidence is not courage; it is blindness to a danger he refuses to fear. The contrast sets humility that sees danger against arrogance that ignores it. This saying, which opens a new section, returns to the theme of fear: the right kind of fear makes a person safe, and the lack of it makes him reckless.
16.notes: In this form the Hebrew verb behind “rages” can mean to be arrogant or to become furious. Here it stands opposite the wise man’s caution: the fool pushes ahead in proud self-assurance. YLT renders it “transgressing,” NASB “arrogant,” and ESV “reckless.” The 1984 NIV supplies “the Lord” as the object of the wise man’s fear in the first line, while the other translations leave the object unstated.

17.brief: Acting in the heat of the moment, a quick-tempered man does foolish things. The man who plots wickedness in cold blood is hated, so both hot anger and calculated malice are condemned.
17.explain:
“A quick-tempered man acts foolishly,”

The quick-tempered man flares up and does foolish things in the heat of the moment. His anger runs ahead of his judgment, and he says and does what he will later regret. Proverbs repeatedly praises the opposite quality, being “slow to anger” (15:18), and this saying shows why. Anger that comes quickly leaves no room for wisdom to speak.

“And a man of wicked intentions is hated.”

The second man is different. He is not hot-tempered but calculating, a man who plots and schemes. People come to hate him, because his malice is deliberate. The two lines are not a simple contrast between good and bad; they set two kinds of wrongdoing side by side. One sins in the heat of the moment, the other in cold blood, and both are condemned. If anything, the second is worse, for the quick-tempered man is called foolish while the schemer is hated.
17.notes:
“Quick-tempered” is literally short of nostrils in Hebrew. The same Hebrew word means both nostrils and anger, so the phrase describes anger that flares quickly. Its opposite appears in 14:29, where “slow to wrath” is literally long of nostrils.

The Hebrew word behind “wicked intentions” means schemes or plans. It can be used positively, as in 1:4, where the NKJV translates it “discretion,” but here it describes plotting.

18.brief: The simple inherit folly, receiving it as their portion simply by drifting along. The prudent are crowned with knowledge, wearing it as an honor they have gained.
18.explain:
“The simple inherit folly,”

The simple, the uncommitted person of 14:15, inherit folly. An inheritance is received rather than earned, and folly comes to the simple in the same way. They do not have to work at becoming foolish; they only have to keep drifting. Without a decision for wisdom, folly becomes their portion by default.

“But the prudent are crowned with knowledge.”

The prudent are crowned with knowledge. A crown is an honor worn in public, and knowledge becomes the prudent person’s honor. The contrast between inheritance and crown is striking. The simple passively receive what comes to them; the prudent wear a reward that marks the life they have chosen. Proverbs does not leave the simple without hope, for Wisdom calls, “O you simple ones, understand prudence” (8:5).

19.brief: In the end the evil will bow before the good, and the wicked will stand waiting at the gates of the righteous. The saying describes the reversal God’s justice brings about over time, even when it is not yet visible.
19.explain:
“The evil will bow before the good,”

The saying looks to the end of things. Those who are evil will finally bow before those who are good. Bowing was a sign of submission and of need, the posture of someone asking for help. The present may show the wicked in power and the good under pressure, but God’s justice reverses that order over time.

“And the wicked at the gates of the righteous.”

The wicked will stand at the gates of the righteous, waiting outside their homes, perhaps asking for help or favor. The picture recalls Joseph’s brothers, who “bowed down before him with their faces to the earth” (Genesis 42:6) when they came to Egypt in need of food. The verse describes the general direction of God’s rule, not a promise that every wrong will be reversed within a person’s lifetime. Its hope is that goodness will finally be vindicated.
19.notes: The Hebrew verb for “bow” is in the form normally used for a completed action, which YLT reflects with “have bowed.” Most translations render it as a future or a general truth. The form presents the outcome vividly, as if already seen, but it does not by itself fix when or how the reversal happens.

20.brief: Here is an honest look at human nature: the poor man is avoided even by his own neighbor, while the rich man has many friends. The saying observes this without approving it, and the next verse calls despising a neighbor sin.
20.explain:
“The poor man is hated even by his own neighbor,”

The saying looks honestly at human nature. The poor man is hated, avoided and treated as a burden, even by his own neighbor, the person who ought to stand with him. Poverty isolates. People keep their distance from someone who may need something from them. Proverbs makes the same observation elsewhere: “All the brothers of the poor hate him” (19:7).

“But the rich has many friends.”

The rich man, by contrast, has many friends. They are drawn to him by what he has and what he can do for them. The saying does not approve of this; it simply describes it. Its honesty prepares for the next verse, which calls despising a neighbor sin (14:21). Placed together, the two sayings first show the world as it is and then show it as God judges it.
20.notes:
The Hebrew of the second line reads literally many are those who love the rich, which NASB and YLT follow. The wording suggests people who attach themselves to the rich for what they can gain.

14:20 and 14:21 both use the Hebrew word for “neighbor,” and the repetition binds the observation to the judgment that follows it.

21.brief: Despising a neighbor is sin, not merely bad manners, and verse 20 has just shown how easily the poor are despised. The one who shows mercy to the poor is truly happy, blessed in the very act of kindness.
21.explain:
“He who despises his neighbor sins;”

After the honest observation of 14:20 comes the moral verdict. To despise a neighbor, to look down on him and treat him as worthless, is sin. It is not merely bad manners or a social misstep. The neighbor in view, given the previous verse, is especially the poor neighbor whom others avoid. God does not share the world’s easy contempt for those who have little.

“But he who has mercy on the poor, happy is he.”

The one who shows mercy to the poor is happy, truly blessed. Mercy here is active kindness and generosity toward those in need. The Hebrew word behind “happy” is the same declaration of blessing that opens the Psalms, “Blessed is the man” (Psalm 1:1), and that Proverbs uses of the one who finds wisdom (3:13). The blessing is not only a future reward; there is joy in the act of kindness itself. Despising the poor is sin, and showing them mercy brings blessing.
21.notes: ESV renders “happy” as “blessed.” The NKJV keeps the Hebrew order by placing “happy is he” at the end of the line.

22.brief: Those who plot evil have already gone astray, as the question expects everyone to admit. Mercy and truth belong to those who plan good, so kindness and faithfulness mark the lives of people who set their minds on doing good.
22.explain:
“Do they not go astray who devise evil?”

The saying begins with a question that expects everyone to agree. Those who plan evil have already wandered off the right path. To “devise” evil is to work it out carefully, the opposite of the impulsive anger of 14:17. Their planning may look clever, but it leads them astray.

“But mercy and truth belong to those who devise good.”

The same verb is used for the other group. They, too, are planners, but they devise good. Mercy and truth belong to them, the steadfast love and faithfulness that God Himself shows and that the father urged his son to keep: “Let not mercy and truth forsake you” (3:3). The line may mean that such people show mercy and truth to others, or that they receive mercy and truth in return; the two belong together. People who set their minds on doing good find their lives marked by kindness and faithfulness.
22.notes:
The Hebrew verb behind “devise” has the basic sense of cutting in, as in engraving or plowing, and from that it comes to mean working out a plan. The same verb appears in “Do not devise evil against your neighbor” (3:29).

ESV renders “mercy and truth” as steadfast love and faithfulness, a pair that runs through the Old Testament as a description of God’s character.

23.brief: Hard work of every kind brings profit. Idle talk, all planning and no doing, leads only to poverty.
23.explain:
“In all labor there is profit,”

Every kind of hard work brings some profit. The Hebrew word for labor suggests painful toil, the kind of effort that costs something. Proverbs does not promise that every task will make a person rich, but it insists that honest work produces something of value. Work done diligently is never wasted.

“But idle chatter leads only to poverty.”

In Hebrew, idle chatter is literally a word of the lips, talk without action. It may be planning, boasting, complaining, or endless discussion of what ought to be done, but nothing comes of it except poverty. The contrast is between doing and only talking about doing. The lazy man of 13:4 wanted much and had nothing; this person talks much and has nothing. Words have their place in Proverbs, but they cannot replace work.
23.notes: KJV renders the second line as the talk of the lips, and ESV has “mere talk.”

24.brief: Riches are pictured as the crown of the wise, an honor that fittingly adorns a life well lived, while the foolishness of fools produces only more folly. Each ends up wearing what he has gathered, though the saying describes wisdom’s fitting reward in general rather than promising wealth to every wise person.
24.explain:
“The crown of the wise is their riches,”

The riches of the wise are pictured as their crown, an honor that suits them. Whatever wealth the wise have, gained honestly and used well, adorns their lives rather than corrupting them. The line follows naturally from 14:23, where labor brings profit, and from 14:18, where the prudent are crowned with knowledge. This is wisdom’s fitting reward in general, not a promise that every wise person will become wealthy.

“But the foolishness of fools is folly.”

The second line is almost a play on words. The foolishness of fools is simply more folly. Whatever fools gather or produce, it adds up to nothing better than folly. The wise wear a crown; fools wear only what they already are. Each ends up with what he has gathered, and the contrast shows that folly can produce nothing beyond itself.
24.notes: The repetition in the second line is deliberate. ESV says folly “brings folly.”

25.brief: A true witness saves lives by telling the truth in court. A deceitful witness speaks lies that can destroy the innocent, so honest testimony can be a matter of life and death.
25.explain:
“A true witness delivers souls,”

The courtroom setting of 14:5 returns. A true witness delivers souls, which here means he saves lives. In Israel a man’s life could depend on what a witness said. An honest witness can rescue an innocent person from death and protect the community from injustice. Telling the truth when it matters is an act that can save lives.

“But a deceitful witness speaks lies.”

The deceitful witness speaks lies; the Hebrew verb behind “speaks” literally means breathes out. Where the true witness saves, the false witness destroys, for his lies can send the innocent to punishment and let the guilty go free. The saying ends the section on a serious note. Truthfulness is not a small virtue; it can be a matter of life and death. Proverbs elsewhere urges, “Deliver those who are drawn toward death” (24:11), and a truthful witness does exactly that.
25.notes:
“Speaks lies” translates the same Hebrew expression used in 14:5, literally breathes out lies, so the two witness sayings bracket the sayings that lie between them.

ESV renders the first line “saves lives.”

26.brief: The fear of the LORD, a right view of God, gives strong confidence rather than anxiety. Those who fear Him are His children, and in Him they have a place of refuge.
26.explain:
“In the fear of the LORD there is strong confidence,”

The fear of the LORD is a right view of God, and the surprise of this saying is what it produces: strong confidence. One might expect fear to make a person anxious, but the fear of the LORD does the opposite. The person who sees God rightly, in His holiness, greatness, and goodness, has nothing else to fear in the same way. Reverence for God becomes the ground of security. The father promised his son, “the LORD will be your confidence” (3:26).

“And His children will have a place of refuge.”

Those who fear the LORD are His children, and in Him they find a place of refuge, a shelter in danger. Fear and confidence belong together here. The same God who is awesome in holiness is the safe place for those who revere Him. “The name of the LORD is a strong tower; The righteous run to it and are safe” (18:10). The section pairs this saying with the next to show the fear of the LORD as both security (14:26) and life (14:27).
26.notes: The Hebrew pronoun in the second line is simply “his,” so it can be read two ways. The NKJV capitalizes “His,” referring to the LORD’s children. ESV and NASB read “his,” referring to the children of the person who fears the LORD, so that a parent’s reverence for God becomes a refuge for the next generation. Both readings are grammatically possible.

27.brief: The fear of the LORD is “a fountain of life,” always flowing and refreshing. It turns a person away from the snares of death, the same thing 13:14 said of the teaching of the wise, because wise teaching and the fear of the LORD go together.
27.explain:
“The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life,”

The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, a spring that keeps flowing and refreshing. It does not give life once and run dry. A right view of God keeps renewing a person, drawing him back to the One who is the source of life. Proverbs said in its opening motto that “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (1:7); here it is also the wellspring of life.

“To turn one away from the snares of death.”

Its purpose is to turn a person aside from the snares of death, the hidden traps along the road. A person who reveres God is kept from paths that look harmless but end in ruin, such as the way that only seems right (14:12). In 13:14 the same words were said of the teaching of the wise. Wise teaching and the fear of the LORD flow from the same source and lead to the same life, for the wise teach what the fear of the LORD has taught them.
27.notes: This verse repeats 13:14 except for its subject: there “The law of the wise is a fountain of life,” here the fear of the LORD.

28.brief: A king’s honor rests on the number of his people, a thriving population under his rule. A prince without people is ruined, so a ruler’s glory depends on the welfare of those he governs.
28.explain:
“In a multitude of people is a king’s honor,”

The final section opens with a saying about kingship. A king’s honor rests on the number of his people. A thriving, growing population under his rule shows that he governs well and that people prosper under him. His glory is bound up with their welfare.

“But in the lack of people is the downfall of a prince.”

A prince without people is ruined. If his subjects are few, whether through oppression, war, famine, or people fleeing his rule, his power collapses. The saying reminds rulers that they exist for the sake of their people, not the other way around. It sets up the section’s other royal saying at 14:35 and its concern with righteousness in a nation (14:34).
28.notes: The sayings about the king in 14:28 and 14:35 frame the last section of the chapter.

29.brief: Being slow to anger shows great understanding. The impulsive person, quick to react, holds up his folly for everyone to see.
29.explain:
“He who is slow to wrath has great understanding,”

The person who is slow to anger shows great understanding. He gives himself time to see the whole situation, to consider the other person’s side, and to respond rather than react. Proverbs links patience with wisdom repeatedly; “The discretion of a man makes him slow to anger” (19:11). Restraint is not weakness; it is understanding at work.

“But he who is impulsive exalts folly.”

The impulsive person, quick to react, “exalts folly.” He lifts it up and puts it on display for everyone to see. Every outburst advertises his lack of judgment. The verse returns to the quick-tempered man of 14:17 and shows the other side: patience is a mark of understanding, and impulsiveness puts folly on a pedestal.
29.notes: “Slow to wrath” is literally long of nostrils in Hebrew, a picture of anger that takes a long time to flare. For the impulsive man the KJV reads hasty of spirit; the Hebrew is literally short of spirit, the opposite of the patient man’s long fuse.

30.brief: A calm and sound heart brings life and health to the whole body. Envy works like rot in the bones, eating away at a person from the inside.
30.explain:
“A sound heart is life to the body,”

A sound heart is a calm, healthy, peaceful heart. Proverbs sees a close connection between the inner life and the body. A heart at peace brings life and health to the whole person, while worry, bitterness, and turmoil can take a physical toll. The saying paints a general truth in poetic terms; it does not promise that a peaceful heart guarantees good health, and it does not mean that every illness comes from envy or anxiety.

“But envy is rottenness to the bones.”

Envy works like rot in the bones, eating away at a person from the inside. Bones in Hebrew thought represent the deepest part of a person’s physical frame, and envy corrupts even there. The envious person resents what others have and is never content with what he has, and that resentment slowly destroys him. Proverbs uses the same picture of the wife who causes shame: she “is like rottenness in his bones” (12:4). The contrast is between a heart at rest and a heart consumed by wanting what belongs to someone else.
30.notes:
“Sound heart” is literally a heart of healing in Hebrew; YLT reads “healed heart.” The Hebrew word for healing is the one translated “health” in 13:17.

NASB renders “envy” as “passion.” The Hebrew word is the ordinary word for jealousy; here it means the resentful wanting of what belongs to someone else.

31.brief: How a person treats the poor is how he treats God. Oppressing the poor insults their Maker, while showing mercy to the needy honors Him (compare Matthew 25:40).
31.explain:
“He who oppresses the poor reproaches his Maker,”

To oppress the poor is to exploit, cheat, or crush those who have little power to defend themselves. Oppression includes unjust practices and systems as well as personal cruelty. The saying makes a startling claim: such a person insults God. The poor man was made by God, and to treat him with contempt is to show contempt for the One who made him. “The rich and the poor have this in common, The LORD is the maker of them all” (22:2).

“But he who honors Him has mercy on the needy.”

The opposite is also true. The one who honors God shows mercy to the needy. Honoring God is not limited to worship; it is expressed in how a person treats the weakest people around him. This line shows that care for the poor is a way of honoring their Maker. Jesus taught the same principle when He said, “inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these My brethren, you did it to Me” (Matthew 25:40).
31.notes:
The first line is closely paralleled in 17:5, “He who mocks the poor reproaches his Maker.”

The Hebrew verb for showing mercy here is the same one used in 14:21 (“has mercy on the poor”), linking the two sayings about the poor in this chapter.

32.brief: The wicked are driven away by their own wickedness when calamity comes. The righteous have a refuge even in death, a security in God that death cannot take away.
32.explain:
“The wicked is banished in his wickedness,”

When calamity comes, the wicked are driven away by their own wickedness. The Hebrew verb behind “banished” pictures being thrust out or pushed down. His evil has no power to hold him up; it is the very thing that drives him out. He has no place to stand when trouble arrives.

“But the righteous has a refuge in his death.”

The righteous man has a refuge even in death. Most likely the saying means that the righteous person’s security in God does not end when life does. Death, which ends everything the wicked trusted in, cannot take away the refuge the righteous have in the LORD. The Old Testament speaks of life beyond death more quietly than the New, but sayings like this point in that direction, and the hope they express finds its fullness in Christ, who has abolished death (2 Timothy 1:10).
32.notes:
The ancient Greek translation of Proverbs, the Septuagint, reads the second line differently, so the hope expressed in “in his death” rests on the Hebrew text. The NKJV and ESV follow the Hebrew text’s “in his death,” and NASB also speaks of the righteous person’s death.

KJV reads “hope” for “refuge” in the second line.

33.brief: Wisdom rests quietly in the heart of a person with understanding and does not need to be shown off. What is in the heart of fools gets made known, because they cannot keep it in.
33.explain:
“Wisdom rests in the heart of him who has understanding,”

Wisdom rests quietly in the heart of a person with understanding. It is settled there, at home, and it does not need to be shown off. The understanding person does not rush to display what he knows; his wisdom comes out when it is needed and serves others rather than impressing them.

“But what is in the heart of fools is made known.”

What is in the heart of fools gets made known. Fools cannot keep it in. Whatever is in them, mostly folly, comes out in their words and actions for everyone to see. The contrast is between wisdom that rests and folly that broadcasts itself, much like 14:24 and 13:16: “a fool lays open his folly.”
33.notes: The second line is difficult, and translations differ. ESV says that wisdom makes itself known even among fools, while NLT adds a negative: “wisdom is not found among fools.” The NKJV, with KJV, reads it as a contrast in which fools reveal what is in them.

34.brief: Righteousness lifts a nation up and gives it honor. Sin brings disgrace to any people, so the moral principle that governs a single life also governs whole peoples.
34.explain:
“Righteousness exalts a nation,”

The principles that govern a single life also govern whole peoples. Righteousness, justice, honesty, and care for the weak, lifts a nation up and gives it honor and stability. The saying does not refer to any particular nation; it states a moral principle that applies to every people under God’s rule.

“But sin is a reproach to any people.”

Sin brings disgrace to any people, whatever its size, wealth, or power. A nation that tolerates injustice, corruption, and oppression brings shame on itself and undermines its own future. The verse follows sayings about the king and about the treatment of the poor (14:28, 31), and it widens the view to a whole society. It is a moral principle for any people, not a slogan for one political party or another.
34.notes:
The Hebrew word translated “reproach” is spelled like the common word for mercy or steadfast love, but here it is a rare word of the same spelling meaning shame or disgrace. Apart from this verse it occurs in Leviticus 20:17 (“it is a wicked thing”). YLT reads it as “goodliness,” producing a very different sense.

The Hebrew behind “any people” is a plural, peoples or nations, so the saying applies to every people, not to one nation only.

35.brief: A king favors a servant who acts wisely. His wrath falls on the one who causes shame, so faithfulness and good sense matter in the service of those in authority.
35.explain:
“The king’s favor is toward a wise servant,”

A king looks favorably on a servant who acts wisely. In the royal court, skill, good judgment, and faithfulness were noticed and rewarded. The saying applies the book’s teaching about wisdom to the world of work and service under authority. A wise servant brings honor to his master and receives honor in return.

“But his wrath is against him who causes shame.”

The king’s anger falls on the servant who causes shame, the one who acts foolishly or dishonestly and so disgraces his master. The chapter that began with a wise woman building her house closes with a wise servant who wins his king’s favor. Faithfulness and good sense matter in every place of service. As a canonical comparison, Jesus’ parable of the talents pictures a master who says, “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25:21).
35.notes: The Hebrew word behind “wise” here describes a servant who acts with insight and prudence, the kind of good sense that serves a master well. ESV and NASB read “deals wisely” or “acts wisely.”
